newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seeks little change in 1997 fish quotas.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks little change in 1997 fish quotas.

text.p: The European Commission outlined on Monday a proposal for little change in most 1997 fish catch quotas, despite a warning earlier this year that sharp cuts were needed in fleets to save threatened stocks.
But its final proposal hinges on the outcome of negotiations which resumed on Monday with Norway on jointly managed herring, mackerel, cod and other important North Sea stocks.

"The Commission is not only obliged...to conserve fish stocks but also to look after the social and economic well-being of fishermen...," David Armstrong, head of the Commission's fisheries conservation unit, told a news briefing.

In May, the EU's executive Commission had warned that there were far too many fishing vessels chasing too few fish and called for cuts of up to 40 percent over the next six years to ensure the long-term survival of the fishing industry.
The proposal provoked uproar in the fishing industry and is set to be watered down after running into fierce resistance from Britain, Spain and other major fishing nations.
"We have this tension between what are on purely scientific grounds fundamentally incompatible (stocks and fishing) aims and we have to form some sort of compromise," Armstrong said.

The Commission has proposed more than 100 total allowable catches (TACs) for different types of fish in different fishing zones. TACs for jointly managed stocks have to be shared with non-EU countries before being allocated among EU member states.
"The majority of TACs are identical," Armstrong said.
But EU and international scientists have warned that stocks of mackerel and North Sea herring as well as plaice and sole were seriously depleted.
The North Sea herring allowable catch was halved to 156,000 tonnes in July after scientists warned that the stock was heading towards extinction.
But scientists have now advised that a 3,000-tonne increase in the North Sea herring catch could be allowed in 1997.

In view of seriously depleted North Sea sole supplies, the Commission is seeking to slash the allowable catch by nearly 50 percent to 12,000 tonnes. A proposal for heavily overexploited North Sea plaice depends on the outcome of Norwegian talks.
Outside the North Sea, the Commission is seeking sharp cuts in 1997 TACs for saithe off the West of Scotland and for hake off Spain to protect depleted stocks.

Armstrong said he was hopeful that agreement could be reached this week with Norway, despite its walk-out of earlier talks in disagreement over herring and mackerel policy, and that it would result in only small cutbacks for most species.
The Commission's proposal will on December 19-20 be discussed by EU fisheries ministers, who each year ease the cuts in order to pacify the angry fishing industry.
With the Commission seeking fewer cuts this year, officials are hopeful that traditional all-night marathon negotiations may not be necessary.
